state.output:
from several places at once. A `VIDEO` surface **references** it by id
(`MEDIA_CONTROLLER_ID`) — the relationship is a reference, not a parent/child
edge; a controller has no children of its own. An audio playback is a controller
with **no** media view, controlled by the application's own views.

- **Protocol**: a leaf node carrying `MEDIA_SOURCE` (0x103B, STRING asset
  reference) and the transport commands — `PLAYBACK_STATE` (0x1035, U32 0/1),
  `MEDIA_POSITION` (0x1036, F32 seconds; a change seeks), `MEDIA_VOLUME`
  (0x1037, F32 0..1), `MEDIA_MUTED` (0x103C, U8), `MEDIA_LOOP` (0x103D, U8),
  `MEDIA_RATE` (0x103E, F32). It is created/deleted like any node, so it
  participates in the structural diff, full-snapshot (`META::RESYNC`), and
  proxy-id remapping with no media-specific machinery.
- **Layout**: **layout-transparent** — no native element, no box, no space, no
  spacing contribution (like `COMMENT` and the `PROXY_VIEW` passthrough,
  [LAYOUT.md](./LAYOUT.md)). Place it for **lifetime stability** (outside any
  swapping branch such as a `VIEW_THAT_FITS` slot), not for layout.
- **Events**: the `MEDIA_*` family targets the controller id, gated by the
  transport properties bound on it (see [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md#media)).
- **Independence**: attaching/detaching a `VIDEO` surface never starts, stops,
  seeks, or re-loads playback; a controller with zero media views keeps playing.
  One controller = one playback, shared by every surface that references it.
- **Kind**: kind-agnostic. A controller referenced by a `VIDEO` surface renders
  video; otherwise the playback is audio (presented by the application's own
  views, never by the protocol).

The full contract — the model, the swap rules, the guards, and the renderer
obligations — is specified in [MEDIA.md](./MEDIA.md).

### Color — `COLOR` 0x03

`Color` mirrors SwiftUI's **dual identity**: it is both a **View** and a
**Data Type** — and it is **never a modifier**.

- **As a View**: a solid-color visual element. It is **layout-greedy** —
  it expands to fill all available space offered by its parent container
  unless explicitly constrained (e.g. by a `.frame`/size modifier). Its color
  `w ≥ T_i`, makes candidate `i` visible and **hides every candidate `j ≠ i`**;
  bands are emitted **ascending** so the highest matching band wins; no band
  exists for `T_0`;
- the per-candidate **default** (below the first band / no match) is candidate
  `0` visible, every other candidate hidden;
- **invariant**: exactly one candidate is visible at every width.

**Hydration collapse (MUST).** After the first `FIT_CHANGED` the app swaps the
slot to the live single-selected-child form (the unselected candidates leave as
`TREE` deltas) and the renderer removes the full-snapshot gating — the gate
markers, the query context, and the band rules — so no CSS gate remains; a
`FIT_CHANGED` that maps to the already-shown candidate re-emits **zero** opcodes.

The collapse is signalled by the **removal of a candidate** (a `TREE` `REMOVE_CHILD`
/`DELETE_NODE` on the slot), not by an arbitrary structural op. A **full-snapshot
emission replayed as opcodes** (e.g. `META::RESYNC`) therefore does **not** collapse
the slot: the renderer reuses its existing gate (the SSR gate markers + band rules)
and keeps showing the width-correct candidate. The app's retained tree stays in the
snapshot form until the first `FIT_CHANGED` downgrade actually removes a candidate.

The concrete web realization (CSS container + per-candidate gate wrappers +
`@container` band rules) is **renderer-owned** and described in
`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/status.md`.

**Shared subtrees in a full snapshot (MUST).** When the same subtree is authored
inside more than one candidate, a full-snapshot emission materializes that subtree
**once per candidate** (each candidate renders its own retained nodes). Every copy
MUST receive a **distinct node id** — no id is reused between candidates, including
nodes with identity-stable semantics such as a media controller
([MEDIA.md](./MEDIA.md)). The frame's unique-node-id invariant
([OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#frame-lifecycle)) therefore holds across the whole slot.

Semantics:
- **Properties**: `FIT_QUERY` (`0x1039`, LIST).
- **Events**: `FIT_CHANGED` (`0x13`, host → guest) — reported fit index.
- **Children**: at most one in the live form; all candidates in a
  full-snapshot emission (the web SSR's first document), in `FIT_QUERY` order.
- **Renderer statelessness**: the measured width and derived index are layout
  output, not retained application state.

### ProxyView — `PROXY_VIEW` 0x1E

A **proxy view**: a transparent container whose child subtree is served by a
**different Pathland server**. It lets one app compose views from several
servers into a single unified document. The proxying server (the app that owns
the proxy node) connects to the origin server as a Pathland **host** (client),
receives the origin's subtree, and splices it into its own stream.

- **Protocol**: a container node with **exactly one** child in the live form —
  the origin subtree's root. The origin subtree's nodes are ordinary nodes of
  the same protocol; the proxying server has **remapped their node ids** into a
  disjoint high range so they never collide with the proxying app's own ids.
- **Layout**: a **transparent passthrough** container. It imposes no spacing or
  alignment of its own; it proposes its own allocated size to its single child
  and, unless the app constrains it (`frame`/size modifiers), sizes to that
  child. Renderers render it as a plain container (a box/`div`) — there is no
  proxy-specific native element.
- **Events**: raw events whose target id falls in a proxy's remapped range are
  the origin server's; the proxying server forwards them (id remapped back) to
  the origin over the origin connection rather than dispatching them locally.
- **Ownership**: the proxy node belongs to the proxying app's retained tree; the
  child subtree belongs to the origin server's retained tree. The proxying app
  never diffs the origin subtree — it forwards the origin's deltas verbatim
  (id-remapped). A **full-snapshot** (`META::RESYNC`) of the proxying app embeds
  the origin's current snapshot; the origin snapshot is requested with a
  `META::RESYNC` sent to the origin server (there is no proxy-specific opcode).
- **Renderer statelessness**: a renderer applies the remapped origin opcodes
  like any other opcodes; it holds no notion of "remote".

The full contract — id namespacing, the snapshot/`RESYNC` handshake, event
routing, SSR embedding, and the backpressure policy — is specified in
[PROXY.md](./PROXY.md).

---

## C. Semantic Control Nodes

Semantic controls encapsulate intent, two-way bindings, accessibility traits,
and local interaction physics. Rendering follows the [Dual-Mode Rendering
Pipeline](#2-dual-mode-rendering-pipeline--platform-delegation): **Native Token
Mode** when the node has no children; **Composite Override Mode** when it does.

Important conflict: `spec/EVENTS.md` and `spec/PRIMITIVES.md` say a full snapshot (META::RESYNC) does NOT collapse the fit slot; the renderer reuses its existing gate. If we add `META::RESET` to the resync answer, the client will have already torn down the SSR gate before applying the snapshot, so the "reuse existing gate" rule would be violated. But on a *reconnect*, the gate was already collapsed by the first FIT_CHANGED (the log shows FIT_CHANGED). On an *initial resync* after reload, the SSR gate is present and RESET would destroy it; the snapshot (server's live collapsed form? `snapshotEmission` true only at mount; the live session's tree was already collapsed by the FIT_CHANGED report sent on open before RESYNC) is single-candidate. Hmm. The CURRENT behavior: on initial resync, the server session mounted with SSR snapshot emission (all candidates) but the client sends FIT_CHANGED on open; when the FIT report is applied, the session collapses to one candidate. If RESYNC arrives before FIT report, the snapshot has all candidates; else collapsed. Either way, if we RESET, the client loses the SSR gate but then builds whatever the snapshot has. Since the snapshot is the live tree (one candidate) after FIT, fine. This is a spec conflict we must explicitly address: update EVENTS.md/PRIMITIVES.md to say the reset-replacement snapshot is the live tree and the renderer rebuilds (gate not reused) — OR use a different mechanism than RESET that preserves the SSR gate.

Hmm, this is important. The spec currently deliberately preserves the SSR fit gate across a resync to avoid "all candidates rendered" and to keep the width-correct candidate. If we reset, we remove the gate; the snapshot must then be the live single-candidate tree. Is it guaranteed? `PathlandSession` mounts with `snapshotEmission(true)`, so the retained tree after mount is the *snapshot form* (all candidates). It only collapses when the app's `fitInput` runs with a FIT_CHANGED. On reconnect/first connect, the client sends FIT_CHANGED on open, so by the time resync is processed (later on the actor), the tree has collapsed to one candidate. Wait: the FIT event is dispatched immediately (not coalesced) and queued before resync, so yes, on a live session the tree is collapsed before resync. On initial resync also the same (onOpen sends FIT before RESYNC). So the resync snapshot is single-candidate. Good. But if no FIT report arrives (e.g., non-web host), the tree stays snapshot form (all candidates) and the snapshot after reset would create all candidates without a gate -> both candidates visible -> the "all branches rendered" bug. Hmm. The `snapshotEmission(true)` is intended for the web first paint only. For a network DOM client, FIT_CHANGED always arrives on open. But a flaky fit observer? Maybe.

Also proxy: `PROXY.md`/PRIMITIVES says a full snapshot of the proxying app embeds the origin snapshot, and the origin's full snapshot does not collapse. With RESET, the client clears the proxy subtree and re-adds the forwarded origin snapshot; the origin snapshot may include all candidates (if the origin is web and its FIT hasn't collapsed). No resume concept. So reconnect = new session is a deliberate design. The snapshot must be a replacement, and media/scroll continuity isn't guaranteed by the protocol. That's acceptable: the app persists state (selected track etc.) so the new session restores UI state; scroll is not persisted. The user only cares that the UI isn't scrambled.

Given that, the simplest robust fix is: **treat a reconnect's snapshot as a full replacement on the client** (clear the retained output before applying it). We can do this without protocol changes by clearing the DOM on reconnect (client-side). But the timing/snapshot identification issue: we can clear on reconnect immediately, before sending ENVIRONMENT/VISIBLE_RANGE/RESYNC. Then all subsequent batches rebuild. Any pre-snapshot deltas no-op. This is essentially a client-initiated RESET. Media/scroll lost, but that's already effectively unavoidable with a new session (scroll definitely, media maybe). And it doesn't conflict with the fit-gate rule? It clears the SSR gate on reconnect, but the snapshot is the new session's live tree (collapsed after FIT), so fine. On initial (non-reconnect) resync, no clear, preserving the existing behavior. 

But wait: clearing on reconnect removes all elements including the scroll container, so the scroll jumps to top; the client then reports visible range 0 (computed from the new empty/rebuilt DOM). The user is scrolled at row 300, reconnect -> top. Not scrambled, but jumps. Is that acceptable? Probably they'd notice. We can preserve scroll with modest effort as described.

Also, clearing on reconnect before the server confirms anything means if the reconnect fails repeatedly, the client shows a blank page. That's worse: a transient failed reconnect would blank the UI. We should only clear when the snapshot actually arrives, not on socket open. But identifying the snapshot... Hmm. We could clear on the first guest→host batch after a reconnect (assuming it's the snapshot). But the first batch may be a pre-snapshot FIT collapse delta (as the log shows seq=1). Clearing then is okay (the snapshot follows). But if the reconnect is to a server that never sends a snapshot? Version mismatch etc. Still.

We can clear right before applying the first guest→host batch after a reconnect. That guarantees no blank on a failed reconnect (unless a partial batch arrives). But if that first batch is a delta from the new session, we clear and apply it to empty (mostly no-op), then the snapshot rebuilds. Good. The scroll position must be captured before clearing (at first batch time, the DOM is still intact). The visible range report is sent at open from the intact DOM (pre-clear). Good. This is a viable no-protocol-change fix:
- Transport: after a reconnect, set `replaceOnNextDelta=true`.
- On the next guest→host (non-heartbeat) batch: call a new `renderer.reset()`/`beginReplacement()` that captures scroll, clears DOM/registry/media/fit state, then apply the batch (which may be a delta or snapshot). Clear flag.
- The server's re-render deltas after reset will progressively rebuild; the snapshot CREATEs everything.
- The lazy range report on open uses the pre-clear scroll/DOM. The server's window may be behind (0..19) unless coalescer flush; but after the snapshot, the client's DOM is rebuilt at top (scroll lost) and it reports 0. Without scroll preservation, the server ends at top. With scroll preservation, it reports 300 and slides. So scroll preservation is needed for UX. But even without, no scramble.

Comparing to snapshot flag + prune: the prune approach keeps elements that are still present, preserving scroll and media, and is less destructive. But the no-protocol client reset is simpler and more decisive. However, clearing on the first delta means dropping the pre-snapshot FIT collapse delta (fine). It also clears if the first batch after reconnect is a PONG? We exclude heartbeat. Good.

But a key concern: the first guest→host batch after reconnect might be a normal delta (if the server reuses the session? no, new session) or the FIT delta. Clearing is safe.

Which approach to recommend? I lean toward the **snapshot flag + prune** as the architecturally correct, least destructive fix, but it requires a protocol flag and has the residual stale-property caveat. The **client reset on reconnect** is simpler, needs no protocol change, and is fully correct (rebuild from a mount stream) but destructive. Given the user's issue is a scramble (not continuity), and the server already creates a new session on reconnect (so continuity is already lost for scroll/media), a client reset on reconnect is honest and simple. But the user might be annoyed by losing scroll position. We can add scroll restoration.

Hmm, actually, wait. Let's reconsider preserving scroll with the client reset. The client clears the DOM at the first post-reconnect batch. At that moment it can record `scrollTop` for all scroll containers by node id. Then it rebuilds from the snapshot. The scroller element gets recreated with the same id (new session pre-order same tree) and can have scrollTop restored. The lazy window reported on open (from the intact DOM) goes to the server via the coalescer; if we also fix the coalescer flush-before-resync, the server snapshot has the right window. Then the rebuilt list at the restored scroll shows the right rows. This is essentially the RESET approach implemented client-side, with scroll preservation. Media: we can preserve media elements (detach rather than destroy) keyed by... their controller id from the new session may differ. Could map by source/role? Too much. Accept playback restart on reconnect (or the app's media service persists).

But hold on: if we don't add the server coalescer flush, a client reset at the first batch (FIT collapse) occurs before the server has applied the visible range (it's coalesced 50ms). The server's snapshot will then be at the top (0..19), and the client rebuilds at top (scroll restored maybe fails because padding/ITEM_COUNT initially zero?). The restored scrollTop may be clamped when content is only top rows; then when the snapshot's lazy window eventually slides, scroll is at 0. So the coalescer flush matters. Include it.

OK, let me settle on a plan that offers the recommended path and mentions the alternatives, and ask the user which they prefer. Since we're in plan mode and shouldn't make big assumptions, I'll use the question tool after presenting the analysis? The instructions for plan mode say ask clarifying questions. I think present the diagnosis and a recommended plan, plus a question on approach (client reset vs snapshot flag/prune) and scope (scroll/media preservation, ADR).

Old DOM's media controller element: the old session closes and should stop/cleanup? Also the paged library source is per service (per session), so pages reload after reconnect (with a 40ms delay each). The persisted state doesn't include scroll. So scroll is lost on a fresh session unless the client preserves it.

## Diagnosis

The scramble is a **reconnect/new-session + snapshot-merge** bug, not a renderer layout bug.

Key chain:

1. Every WebSocket reconnect gets a **new `uiId`**, and therefore a **brand-new server session/tree** (`PathlandRegistry.java:244-258`, `PathlandSpring`/Quarkus sockets). Node ids restart at 1 and a lazy list mounts at its default top window (`LazyList.kt:336-346`).
2. The client asks for a snapshot, but applies it as an **in-place merge**:
   - `CREATE_NODE` reuses any existing element by id (`apply.ts:715-731`)
   - `INSERT_CHILD` skips when the child is already present (`apply.ts:747-783`)
   - the snapshot never deletes nodes that the new tree doesn't contain
3. There is **no removal of the old lazy window**, so the pre-disconnect rows stay in the DOM while the new session's rows are created from a different window/id-space. The lazy padding is then recomputed from the new `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` (`apply.ts:2494-2576`) over the mixed child list — that is the visible scramble.
4. Two aggravators:
   - On connection open the client calls `refreshLazyWindows(renderer)` **without `force`** (`index.ts:142`), so an unchanged range is not re-sent after reconnect (despite ADR-0017/status saying connection-open reports are immediate).
   - The server coalesces `VISIBLE_RANGE` for ~50 ms (`VisibleRangeCoalescer.java:59-90`), so `RESYNC` routinely renders **before** the client's current window is applied. The new session therefore snapshots the top window while the browser is at row ~300.
5. Each reconnect repeats this, accumulating more stale rows; the resulting child-count/visible-range thrash plausibly explains the 1337-op bursts and the repeated 15 s watchdog reconnects.

Supporting contract: `spec/OPCODE.md:479` and `845-850` say a snapshot must converge to the same tree as a fresh snapshot; the current client merge cannot do that once the new tree's ids/window diverge.

## Recommended fix (no protocol change): replacement on reconnect

Treat the first post-reconnect delta batch as a signal to discard the renderer's retained output and rebuild from the resync snapshot.

1. **Client replacement**
   - Export a `resetRenderedOutput(renderer)` from `apply.ts` (reuse/extend `CMD_RESET` cleanup, `purgeSubtreeRegistry`, media/fit observer cleanup).
   - In `Transport`, after a reconnect, set `replacementPending`; on the first non-heartbeat guest→host batch, reset the renderer, then apply the batch.
   - This is a renderer-output cache reset, not application state; the new session's mount stream is authoritative.

2. **Preserve scroll (recommended)**
   - In `resetRenderedOutput`, capture `scrollTop/scrollLeft` for scroll containers keyed by node id.
   - Restore those offsets after the rebuilt node of that id exists (end of `applyBatch`), then force one lazy refresh so the correct `VISIBLE_RANGE` is reported.

3. **Force ranges on open**
   - `index.ts:142`: `refreshLazyWindows(renderer, true)` on every open (before the reconnect `RESYNC` is sent, which `transport.ts:165-183` already orders correctly).

4. **Flush pending ranges server-side before resync**
   - Add `VisibleRangeCoalescer.drain(sessionId)`; in `PathlandRegistry.resync` (and the existing-session `open` path), dispatch the latest pending range to the session **before** `session.resync()`.
   - This makes the snapshot render at the window the client is actually viewing instead of the default top window.

5. **Tests**
   - TS: old DOM at window ~300 + reconnect replacement + snapshot from a fresh tree at window ~300 → no duplicate/stale lazy rows, correct child count/padding.
   - TS: reconnect re-reports a range even when it is unchanged; scroll offsets survive replacement.
   - Java: coalesced range is applied before `resync`, and the snapshot's `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` matches it.
   - Java/TS: snapshot after a same-session sequence gap also replaces cleanly.

6. **Docs/status**
   - Update `lib/typescript/status.md` (replace the "resync replays without clobbering" note with "SSR hydration merges; reconnect/gap replacement resets and rebuilds") and `lib/java/pathland-server-core/status.md` (range drain + replacement semantics).
   - `spec/OPCODE.md`: clarify that a resync snapshot is authoritative and a renderer may discard retained output after reconnect/session replacement (implementation behavior, not a wire change).

7. **Rebuild shipped bundle**
   - Run `mvn -P refresh-ide validate` (or the design/build + `copy-to-libs` path) so the content-hashed `dom-renderer-*.js` in the Spring/Quarkus jars includes the fix.

## Alternatives considered

- **Snapshot batch flag + prune unseen nodes** (add `FLAG_SNAPSHOT`): preserves DOM/scroll/playback and fit gates, but adds a protocol flag and still cannot clear stale property/text state on merged ids.
- **Server emits `META::RESET` before the snapshot**: simplest semantics, but destroys scroll/playback and conflicts with `spec/EVENTS.md:337-344` / `PRIMITIVES.md` (snapshot must not collapse the SSR fit gate). Not recommended.

## Verification

- `cd lib/typescript && npm test && npm run typecheck`
- `cd lib/java && mvn -P jvm-only test`
- Manual: Spring demo, scroll the library deep, force a disconnect (DevTools offline / restart server), confirm no duplicated/mixed rows, and confirm whether scroll is retained; watch server logs for send failures / resync loops.

No web-framework dependency — framework glue lives in the starters. ## Implemented - **Security hardening (issue #63)**: `WindowIds` validates the client-supplied `wid` (≤128 chars, `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`; a colon is rejected so it cannot collide with the mount-qualified state scope). Invalid ids are treated as absent (SSR defaults) or replaced with a fresh UUID on the WebSocket. `InboundRateLimiter` bounds inbound batches/bytes per connection before actor work is queued (`pathland.max-inbound-batches-per-second`, default 500; `pathland.max-inbound-bytes-per-second`, default 2 MiB) and reports drops via `PathlandTelemetry.inboundDropped` (`pathland.inbound.dropped`). The SSR script tag now carries `integrity="sha384-…"` from the manifest's second line (`PathlandAssets.bundleIntegrity()`); an older one-line manifest simply omits it. - **Attributed text transport**: `FrameRebase` rebases `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`'s string-section offset (like `SET_TEXT`) for delta batching/frame merging, and `ProxyIdMap` remaps its node id. - **Window metadata + SSR head attrs**: `PathlandSession.renderHtml` injects host attrs into the renderer's opening `` (which now carries `lang`), and `FrameRebase` rebases `SET_WINDOW_METADATA` string offsets. Proxy origin metadata is dropped with the other META opcodes. - **Per-route SEO metadata (issue #45)**: `PageMetadata`/`PageMetadataRequest` carry canonical URL, Open Graph/Twitter cards, and JSON-LD. `PathlandApp` gains a default `pageMetadata(request)` hook (active mount-stripped route + host canonical URL); `PathlandRegistry.renderHtml(route, wid, hostDefaults)` merges host defaults with the app's per-route overrides before SSR. Existing overloads keep the legacy head. - **`PathlandApp`** — the app's root-view factory (`View newRoot()` + optional `theme()`); the single app-specific piece a starter needs. - **`MountedApp`** — `record MountedApp(String path, PathlandApp app)`: one app mounted at a subpath prefix (normalized; `/` = root). Hosts any number of them. - **`PathlandHost`** — the multi-app dispatcher: one `PathlandRegistry` per mounted app (own actor thread, own sessions). `match(requestUri)` resolves the owning registry by **longest mount-prefix match** and reports the **mount-stripped route** (a root mount claims every unclaimed path). Duplicate mount paths are rejected at construction. - **`PathlandRegistry`** — session lifecycle per app: single actor thread, 1:1 sessions keyed by a **per-connection `uiId`** (a fresh id per WebSocket connection, so two windows of the same browser never share a UI model), lazy creation on first environment message, pending connections (each carrying the mount-prefixed state scope from the client's per-window `wid`), `open(uiId, wid, conn)`/`environment`/`dispatch`/`resync`/`close`/`renderHtml`/`shutdown`. Inbound `VISIBLE_RANGE` events are coalesced latest-wins per `(session, target)` for ~50 ms (`VisibleRangeCoalescer`, ADR-0017); other events dispatch - immediately. `VisibleRangeCoalescerTest` covers latest-wins/close, and - `VisibleRangeRegistryTest` proves a paged lazy list loads and renders only the - settled window after a burst. New: + immediately. `resync` (and the message-before-open `open` attach path) **drains + the session's pending coalesced ranges and applies them before the snapshot**, so + a reconnecting client's current window is honored instead of a fresh session's + default top window. `VisibleRangeCoalescerTest` covers latest-wins/drain/close, + and `VisibleRangeRegistryTest` proves a paged lazy list loads and renders only + the settled window after a burst, including resync-before-coalescer-flush. New: - `mountPath()`/`base()` — each app's framework base is `//_pathland` (`/_pathland` for the root), emitted as `data-pathland-base` in SSR; - `stateScope(windowId)` — app-qualified state-store scope (`mount:wid`) so apps and windows sharing a store never collide; - `stripRoute(route)` — strips the mount prefix from SSR routes, WS environment ROUTE fields, **and inbound `NAVIGATE` URLs** (browser back/forward sends the real address, e.g. `http://host/app2/home`), so a mounted app always sees its own route space (`/app2/home` → `/home`). `Router.pathOf` is reused for URL→path extraction. - `shutdown()` — serialized on the actor and idempotent: work enqueued after shutdown starts is dropped, sessions are closed on the actor thread, then the executor is stopped and awaited. Teardown can no longer race a queued mount/resync mutating the same emitter (regression-tested by `shutdownSerializesWithQueuedActorWork`). - **Topic subscriptions / external UI updates**: `PathlandSignalHub` (one per mount) routes `publish(topic, subject, value)` only to sessions subscribed to that exact `(topic, subject)` pair (global topics use the reserved `GlobalSubject` singleton and the two-argument `publish(topic, value)` overload; still only subscribed sessions update); `SessionSubscriptions` holds each session's local mirror, coalesces publishes latest-wins, schedules one actor drain, and unregisters on close/unsubscribe. `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` hands arbitrary work to the session actor from any thread; a session context is installed around every actor task (mount, dispatch, drain, theming) so `topic(...)` resolves during render. `SessionContext.isLive()` distinguishes a live session from a one-shot SSR render, and `SessionContext.onClose(...)` registers cleanup (data sources, …) that `PathlandSession.close()` runs after unsubscribing. `PathlandHost.signalHub()`/`signalHub(mount)` expose the hub. Telemetry: `topics.published`/`coalesced`/`dropped`. See `docs/external-updates.md` and `TopicsTest`. - **Per-window isolation (no session cookie)**: session identity (the `uiId` map key) is deliberately separate from the persisted-state scope (the client's `wid`, carried only on the WebSocket URL — never in the page URL, so the address bar stays clean). The SSR request therefore has no `wid`: `renderHtml(route, wid)` with a null `wid` renders defaults; the client's live session is scoped by the WS `wid`, and a same-tab reload re-syncs that window's persisted state over the WebSocket. The old `session` cookie is removed. - **`PathlandSession`** — per-session: builds the `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH` signal, mounts `app.newRoot().modifiers(environmentBinding(e -> e.key(ACTIVE_PATH).value(activePath)))`, **delta-batched send-on-`endFrame`** (`DeltaBatcher` coalesces per-signal frames into one batch — flush ~20 ms or 16 KB, string offsets rebased — so a continuous input burst can't overflow a remote WebSocket send queue), `applyEnvironment` (re-route guard-aware via the bound router), `dispatch` (tap/nav-intent/text/value/date/NAVIGATE), `resync`, `renderHtml`, `close`. Runtime theming: `setTheme(ThemeData)`, `resetTheme()`, and `setColorScheme(ThemeMode)` emit one `META::RESET_THEME` + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` frame or `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` to the live client (renderer state; no tree re-emission). The SSR document keeps the mount theme until a resync/reload. `sendBatch` drops the connection on any send failure (a client reconnect then re-syncs via `META::RESYNC` instead of silently stalling on an "open" socket); `closeConnection` best-effort closes an `AutoCloseable` adapter (the starters now close their underlying WebSocket on failure). Now takes the app's `base` and `stateScope` explicitly (the registry supplies them). - **`DeltaBatcher`** — merges session delta frames (opcodes + a single rebased string section) and flushes as one network batch on a timer/byte threshold; the Java analogue of the Rust transport's `Batcher`. It owns the per-session **message sequence** (stamped on each flushed batch via `FrameCodec.encodeFrame(frame, sequence)`) so the DOM client can detect a lost batch and recover with `META::RESYNC` (spec/OPCODE.md §Sequence gap detection); an empty flush consumes no sequence. The **sender runs OUTSIDE the monitor** — a blocking/queueing send can never stall the actor thread's `append` or the flush scheduler. Coalescing tests cover merging + rebasing, a 100-frame burst collapsing to one send, incrementing sequences, and a blocking sender not holding the lock. - **`PathlandConnection`** — the transport seam (`send(byte[])`/`isOpen()`); each starter adapts its WebSocket type to it. - **Observability seam** — `PathlandTelemetry` (default `NOOP`): the runtime emits session open/close, inbound event batches, inbound drops (oversize/rate), flushed batches (frames/opcodes/bytes + merge-encode time), SSR render latency, resync requests, and send failures; the host binds a pull-based active-sessions gauge. `PathlandHost`/`PathlandRegistry`/ `PathlandSession`/`DeltaBatcher` thread it through (a host with no telemetry pays nothing). This module also ships the `dev.pathland.observability` Micrometer + OpenTelemetry adapters; the starters auto-wire them. Logging is **SLF4J** (both frameworks bind it) — the old ad-hoc `System.out` is gone. See issue #62. - **Concurrency stress** — `RegistryConcurrencyTest`: 100 sessions driven through the registry concurrently (clicks on each session's button) while SSR-style requests construct throwaway sessions on request threads — the shared-actor / global-`Scheduler` cross-session corruption guard. Each session must reach exactly its own click count (no lost effects, no cross-session values). - **Shared WS test harness** — `dev.pathland.server.test.{WsSession,MultiSessionProbe}` (a JDK-WebSocket client speaking the PLPL protocol: env/resync/click/ping) lives in this module in main scope, so package builds resolve it as a normal jar; the starters' 100-session stress tests reuse it. - **State stores** — the starters default to `InMemoryStateStore` (or an app-provided `StateStore` bean). Redis is opt-in via the separate `pathland-state-redis` module (`RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback`), so server runtimes and native-image builds that use in-memory state never carry Lettuce. - **Observability adapters** — `dev.pathland.observability.MicrometerTelemetry` turns the seam into `pathland.*` meters (counters, timers, a distribution summary, a pull-based sessions gauge, every meter tagged by `mount`); the optional `TracingTelemetry` decorator emits an OpenTelemetry span per frame send / inbound event batch / SSR render. Micrometer is a compile dependency; the OTel API is `optional`, so a host that does not enable tracing pays nothing. - **SSR debug comments (property-gated)**: `PathlandSession`/`PathlandRegistry` take a `debugHtml` flag (constructor + `isDebugHtml()`); when set, `renderHtml` uses the renderer's debug mode so every rendered node is prefixed with an HTML comment naming its component and the modifiers applied. The Spring/Quarkus starters bind it to the `pathland.debug-html` property (default `false`). - **Reserved framework root**: `PathlandSession.PATHLAND_BASE` (`/_pathland`) — the SSR page carries the app's base as `data-pathland-base` and the DOM-client bundle is injected at `{base}/dom-renderer-.js` (`PathlandAssets` reads the current name from the `_pathland/dom-renderer.current` manifest on the classpath — shipped in the Spring Boot starter (`static/_pathland/`) and the Quarkus extension (`META-INF/resources/_pathland/`) — resolving through the thread context classloader first so an application-supplied override wins; it falls back to the literal `dom-renderer.js` only when absent) so the client's WebSocket and asset refs resolve from the same reserved prefix (spec DSL.md). The content-hashed name busts the immutable asset cache with a fresh URL per build. The built-in base design is linked the same way: `renderHtml` renders through `HtmlRenderer.renderLinked(frame, root, base)`, so the CSS href is `{base}/base-.css` (token overrides/fit rules stay inline). Multi-app hosts give each mount its own base. - **Per-window-id service worker (opt-in, issue #155)**: `PathlandHost` carries a host-level `serviceWorker` flag (default `false`; one registration covers the whole origin) threaded to every `PathlandRegistry`; `PathlandSession.renderHtml` emits `data-pathland-service-worker="true"` on `` when set, and the DOM client registers `{base}/sw.js` (root scope) / unregisters when absent (the kill switch). `PathlandRegistry.serviceWorkerUrl()` names the served script. `renderHtml` also emits `data-pathland-ssr-scoped="true"` when the request carried a real per-window id, so the client can skip its initial `META::RESYNC` (the SSR was already rendered with that window's state and the live session shares it). ## Not implemented / gaps - No multi-node/shared sessions (each server owns its sessions in-memory). - Topic fan-out is node-local: `PathlandSignalHub` routes to this process's sessions only. A Redis/pub-sub-backed hub (each node fanning out to its local sessions) is a follow-up; the topic name + subject are the stable wire keys. - Quarkus mounted-app WebSocket endpoints require a **single-segment** mount path (the `/{app}` path param); Spring supports any depth. - **Virtualized lazy stacks (ADR-0014)**: SSR emits the engine's first window (default 20 rows) and the full virtual extent; `VISIBLE_RANGE` input routes through `InputDispatcher`, and the session binds `Platform.VIEWPORT` (updated by `META::ENVIRONMENT`) for hosts that know the surface size at mount. Pure + unit-tested. - **`proxy.ProxyTransport`** + **`proxy.JdkWebSocketTransport`** — the outbound connection seam (default: the JDK `HttpClient` WebSocket client, no new dependency) with a `Factory` so a starter can swap a native client. - **`proxy.ProxySession`** — one origin connection: starts with a `META::PING` readiness probe, waits for the origin's transport-level `META::PONG`, then sends `META::ENVIRONMENT` + `META::RESYNC` (the probe avoids racing the origin's `@OnOpen`/session wiring), **remaps** the origin snapshot into the proxy's block and attaches the origin root under the proxy node, forwards live deltas remapped, routes client events back (target unmapped), replies `PONG` to origin `PING`, translates origin `META::RESET` into a **scoped** subtree teardown (never a global reset), tears the subtree down on disconnect (the origin session is per-connection), and reconnects with exponential backoff. A lost probe/`RESYNC` is retried from the proxy scheduler starting at 50 ms and backing off to 500 ms until the snapshot arrives, so a lost first handshake cannot consume the whole SSR budget. The service credential + a cycle-guard instance id ride the handshake headers. **Backpressure** (spec/PROXY.md §8): a "chatty origin" breaker (a per-second batch cap → drop + `RESYNC`) and event coalescing (pointer-moves coalesce by target; discrete events flush immediately). - **`proxy.ProxyHost`** — one `ProxySession` per `PROXY_VIEW` node, each with its own block; routes inbound events whose target is in a proxy range to the owning origin connection; owns the proxy scheduler. `reconcile(wanted)` starts a session for every `PROXY_VIEW` node and closes the session of every node that left the tree; released id blocks go to a **free-block pool** and are reused, so repeated removal/re-add cycles never exhaust the 1024-block range. - **`PathlandSession`** integration — captures `RenderResult.proxyViews()` and registers the emitter's structural-reconcile callback (`Emitter.onStructureReconciled`) to `reconcileProxies()`, so a proxy lives **exactly while its node is in the retained tree** (spec/PROXY.md §7): a `ViewThatFits` slot dropping the candidate that held it closes the origin connection, and re-adding it opens a fresh one (re-seeded by `META::RESYNC`). The host's frames feed the session's `DeltaBatcher` (a single unified sequence); `dispatch` splits proxy-range events to the origin and everything else to the app's own bindings; `close` tears the proxies down. `proxyTransportFactory(...)` lets a host supply a framework transport. - **`PathlandTelemetry`** — `proxyConnected`/`proxyDisconnected`/`proxyBatchDropped`/ `proxyResyncRequested` (all default no-ops). **SSR embed (M2).** `renderHtml` starts the proxies and **blocks** for each origin's snapshot (`ProxySession.awaitSnapshot`, bounded by a 2s timeout), then splices the remapped origin frames into the session's mount frame (`FrameMerger`, reusing the batcher's string rebasing via `FrameRebase`) so the renderer emits **one** document — the origin subtree plus its fit band rules in the same head. The origin's **global** token overrides (`SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`) are **dropped** (live + SSR): a proxied app renders under the **host's** theme, while its token *references* resolve against that theme (spec/PROXY.md §9). A proxy whose origin does not answer in time renders empty (a placeholder) and hydrates over the live connection. A client `META::RESYNC` also replays A's tree **and** asks every origin for a fresh snapshot (`ProxyHost.resyncAll`). **Gaps (M3):** nested proxies and per-proxy theme scoping are deferred (the origin's global overrides are dropped, not scoped, spec/PROXY.md §9). A tiny orphan window remains on removal: an origin batch already queued in the `DeltaBatcher` (≤20 ms) when the proxy node is removed can still create an unattached element in the client's `byId` (not in the DOM); eliminating it needs the `ProxySession` to track the ids it emitted and `DELETE` them on close. ## Verified by `mvn test` — `PathlandSessionTest`: mounts + routes taps through the binding maps, `applyEnvironment`/`resync`/`close` idempotent, registry SSR + lifecycle/teardown, **two windows with the same `wid` still get separate sessions** (a tap to one never reaches the other), and  # Pathland Opcode Protocol Specification
 
 **Wire protocol version:** 1
 **Status:** Draft
 **Format:** Fixed-size (16-byte) opcode engine
 **Machine-readable IDs:** `spec/protocol.tsv`
 **Last Updated:** November 1, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## Overview
 
 The Pathland Opcode Protocol is the **fixed-size instruction engine** at the heart of the Rust-first architecture. The **opcode engine** emits the application's **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding, alignment — as a stream of fixed 16-byte opcodes into a **ring buffer** in **linear memory**. The host renderer consumes the ring and maps the structure onto that platform's **native elements** (GTK4 widgets, DOM elements, HTML).
 
 **The engine does not compute layout and does not emit rects.** Native renderers lay out their own native elements from the constraint properties the engine passes through. This is the Pathland principle: *always render through that platform's native elements.*
 
 This specification supersedes the historical variable-length binary instruction format (which has been removed from the repository).
 
 The concrete numeric IDs are also emitted as the target-neutral `protocol.tsv`
 manifest from the canonical Rust constants; language bindings validate their
 hand-written constants against it. The prose tables remain authoritative for
 semantics, the manifest for exact wire numbers.
 
 ### Goals
 
 **Decision rationale:** [fixed-width binary instructions and transport-independent
 frames](../docs/decisions/0001-fixed-width-binary-protocol.md),
 [native declarative layout](../docs/decisions/0002-native-declarative-layout.md),
 and [application-owned state and deltas](../docs/decisions/0003-application-state-and-delta-emission.md).
 The requirements and wire definitions remain in this specification and its companions.
 
 - **Sub-millisecond execution**: every opcode is a fixed 16 bytes; emission is a diff over the retained tree with **zero dynamic heap allocations** in the steady state.
 - **L1 CPU cache alignment**: a 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes**. Ring slots are 16-byte aligned and densely packed.
 - **Reactive emission**: only the nodes that changed emit opcodes. An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes (see [Reactive Emission](#reactive-emission)).
 - **Linear, deterministic decoding**: the host walks the ring with a single cursor.
 
 ### Core Principles
 
 1. **Fixed-size instructions**: every opcode is exactly 16 bytes — no length prefixes, no skippable-variable framing.
 2. **Declarative, not positioned**: the engine describes *what* the UI is (stacks, text, constraints), never *where* it is. Native elements compute their own positions.
 3. **Numeric IDs**: categories, commands, component types, and properties are numeric.
 4. **Native elements**: renderers map the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 5. **Zero-copy**: the ring and arena are plain regions of the same linear memory shared with the host.
 6. **Single-producer / single-consumer**: the guest engine produces; the host renderer consumes. No locks required.
 
 ---
 
 ## Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 | Field | Size | Offset | Description |
 |-------|------|--------|-------------|
 | `Category` | 1B | 0 | Opcode category (see [Category Table](#category-table)) |
 | `Command` | 1B | 1 | Command within the category (see [Command Tables](#command-tables)) |
 | `Flags` | 2B | 2 | Category/command-specific flags |
 | `A` | 4B | 4 | Primary payload |
 | `B` | 4B | 8 | Secondary payload |
 | `C` | 4B | 12 | Tertiary payload |
 
 All multi-byte values are **little-endian**. The Rust reference type is `#[repr(C, packed)]`:
 
 ```rust
 #[repr(C, packed)]
 pub struct Opcode {
     pub category: u8,
     pub command: u8,
     pub flags: u16,
     pub a: u32,
     pub b: u32,
     pub c: u32,
 }
 ```
 
 `size_of::<Opcode>() == 16`.
 
 ### Payload encoding conventions
 
 - **Float payloads** (`spacing`, `padding`, sizes) are stored as raw `f32` (IEEE 754) bit patterns in a `u32` field.
 - **Signed payloads** (the `I32` value type, and dedicated commands like `SET_DATE`'s days-since-epoch) are stored as the raw two's-complement bit pattern of a signed value in a `u32` field; a consumer reinterprets the field as `i32`.
 - **Node IDs** are `u32`.
 - **Component types / property IDs** are `u16`; when packed into a 4-byte payload they occupy the low two bytes (the high bytes are reserved / zero unless documented).
 - **Arena references** are a `u32` byte offset into the arena region (see [Arena](#arena)).
 - **Colors** are packed `0xAARRGGBB` in sRGB (see [Colors](#colors)).
 
 ### Reserved ranges
 
 - `Category == 0` is reserved (invalid).
 - `Command == 0` in any category is reserved (invalid).
 - `Category 0x80-0xFF`: custom/extended categories.
 
 ---
 
 ## Category Table
 
 | Category | Value | Name | Producer | Description |
 |----------|-------|------|----------|-------------|
 | `TREE` | `0x01` | Tree mutations | Guest engine | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | `PARAMETER` | `0x02` | Constraints & tokens | Guest engine | Property values (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | `EVENT` | `0x03` | Raw inputs | Host renderer | Pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | `META` | `0x04` | Control | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |
 
 ---
 
 ## Command Tables
 
 ### TREE (0x01)
 
 The `componentType` values (the primitive views the protocol supports) are
 catalogued in [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md), grouped by their SwiftUI
 counterpart. Component IDs are allocated there spec-first; this file remains
 the wire-format authority.
 
 | Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | Description |
 |---------|-------|---|---|---|-------|-------------|
 | `CREATE_NODE` | `0x01` | nodeId | componentType (u16, low) | 0 | — | Create a node of `componentType` |
 | `DELETE_NODE` | `0x02` | nodeId | 0 | 0 | — | Delete a node and its subtree |
 | `INSERT_CHILD` | `0x03` | parentId | childId | index | — | Insert `childId` into `parentId` at `index`; append is `index = u32::MAX` (`APPEND`) |
 | `REMOVE_CHILD` | `0x04` | parentId | childId | 0 | — | Remove `childId` from `parentId` |
 | `MOVE_CHILD` | `0x05` | parentId | childId | newIndex | — | Move child to `newIndex` (after removal); append is `newIndex = u32::MAX` (`APPEND`) |
 
 ### PARAMETER (0x02)
 
 The engine does not emit positions. `PARAMETER` carries the **constraint properties**
 that native renderers feed to their own layout — spacing, alignment, FILL/HUG
 size hints — plus **styling modifiers** (padding, colors, fonts, borders).
 
 | Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | Description |
 |---------|-------|---|---|---|-------|-------------|
 | `SET_PROPERTY` | `0x01` | nodeId | propertyId (u16, low) + valueType (u8, high byte) | value | — | Set a constraint/style property; `value` depends on `valueType` |
 | `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` | `0x02` | arenaRef (path) | valueType (u8) | value | — | Override a design token; path is an arena string |
 | `SET_TEXT` | `0x03` | nodeId | arenaRef (utf8) | 0 | — | Set a node's text content |
 | `SET_DATE` | `0x04` | nodeId | days since epoch (I32) | millis of day (U32) | — | Set a node's date value (e.g. a `DATE_PICKER`); see [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md#date) for the matching `DATE_CHANGED` event |
 | `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` | `0x05` | nodeId | arenaRef (payload) | 0 | — | Set a node's text content plus style runs and links; payload format below |
 
 `SET_PROPERTY` encodes the value type in the **high byte of `B`** (bits 24–31) and the property id in the low two bytes:
 
 ```
 B = (valueType << 16) | propertyId
 ```
 
 #### Value types
 
 | Value Type | Value | C / value encoding |
 |------------|-------|--------------------|
 | `U8` | `0x01` | low byte of C |
 | `U32` | `0x02` | u32 |
 | `I32` | `0x03` | i32 |
 | `F32` | `0x04` | f32 |
 | `STRING` | `0x05` | arenaRef (utf8) |
 | `ENUM` | `0x06` | low byte of C |
 | `COLOR` | `0x07` | packed `0xAARRGGBB` |
 | `DESIGN_TOKEN` | `0x08` | arenaRef (token path) |
 | `LIST` | `0x09` | arenaRef (length-prefixed array, see below) |
 
 > **Enum-valued properties** (`ALIGNMENT`, `TEXT_ALIGNMENT`, `TRUNCATION_MODE`,
 > `ROLE`, `STATE`, and the draft `FONT_*`/`CONTENT_MODE`/`CONTROL_SIZE`/`SHAPE_KIND`
 > properties) are carried with the **`F32` value type**, holding the numeric enum
 > code as an f32 bit pattern (e.g. `ALIGNMENT=Center(1)` → `C = 1.0f32.to_bits()`).
 > The enumerated code tables live in
 > [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md#appendix-enumerated-values). The `ENUM` value type
 > (low byte of `C`) is available for explicitly `ENUM`-coded properties.
 >
 > **Token references**: any property that normally carries a `COLOR` / `F32` /
 > `STRING` / `ENUM` value MAY instead carry the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type, with
 > `C` = arenaRef to a token path (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)
 > and [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md)).
 >
 > **`LIST` arrays**: a `LIST` value (`C` = arenaRef) is a length-prefixed array in
 > the string arena: `[u32 count][element × count]`, each element a `u32` holding
 > the value-type's bit pattern — currently produced with each element a `F32`
 > (the `FIT_QUERY` threshold table), so `bytes = 4 + 4·count`. The count is the
 > first `u32` (little-endian); a zero count is an empty list. Decoders read the
 > element count, never infer it from the arena length, so a property can re-emit
 > a shorter list with the arena entry intact.
 
 #### Attributed text payload (`SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`)
 
 `PARAMETER::SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` (`0x05`) sets a node's text together with
 range-scoped style runs and links. The opcode stays 16 bytes: `B` references a
 single length-prefixed arena entry (absolute offset over the shared ring,
 *relative* offset into the batch's string section over the network — the same
 dual convention as `SET_TEXT`). The payload is binary, not UTF-8:
 
 ```
 [u32 textByteLen][utf8 text]
 [u32 runCount]
   repeat runCount:
     [u32 start][u32 end][u32 attrCount]
     repeat attrCount:
       [u16 propId][u8 valueType][u8 reserved = 0][u32 value]
 [u32 linkCount]
   repeat linkCount:
     [u32 start][u32 end][u32 urlByteLen][utf8 url]
 ```
 
 All integers are little-endian. `start`/`end` are **UTF-8 byte offsets** into
 `text`, half-open `[start, end)`. A decoder MUST reject (ignore the opcode) when
 a range is not on a UTF-8 boundary or `end > textByteLen`.
 
 Style runs carry the **text-format property vocabulary** from
 [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md#2-text-formatting). V1 allows these scalar
 attributes only:
 
 | Property | ID | `valueType` | Value |
 |----------|----|-------------|-------|
 | `FONT_SIZE` | `0x1007` | `F32` (`0x04`) | points |
 | `FONT_WEIGHT` | `0x1008` | `F32` (`0x04`) | 100–900 |
 | `COLOR` | `0x100A` | `COLOR` (`0x07`) | `0xAARRGGBB` |
 | `FONT_STYLE` | `0x1017` | `F32` (`0x04`) | `Normal`=0, `Italic`=1 |
 | `FONT_DESIGN` | `0x1018` | `F32` (`0x04`) | `Default`=0, `Serif`=1, `Rounded`=2, `Monospaced`=3 |
 | `UNDERLINE` | `0x101F` | `U8` (`0x01`) | `0`/`1` |
 | `STRIKETHROUGH` | `0x1020` | `U8` (`0x01`) | `0`/`1` |
 
 `FONT_FAMILY` (`STRING`), `TEXT_STYLE`, `LINE_SPACING`, design-token references,
 and effects are **not** valid run attributes in v1 (runs carry scalar values
 only). A decoder ignores an unknown `propId` or unsupported `valueType`; it never
 errors the frame.
 
 Links are a separate section so style runs stay scalar-only. A link carries only
 its URL in v1; renderers own link presentation. Links and runs may overlap; the
 node's own text-format properties remain the base, and a run overrides the
 properties it sets for its range. Where multiple covering runs set the same
 property, the **later run in wire order wins**. Where multiple links cover a
 character, the later link wins.
 
 A renderer that does not implement rich text MUST still render the payload's
 `text` as plain text. The plain text is also the fallback when a payload fails
 validation. `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` supersedes `SET_TEXT` for the node: an engine
 that emits the attributed form does not also emit `SET_TEXT` for the same state.
 
 #### Constraint properties for native layout
 
 The following properties drive native layout; the renderer maps them to its
 native layout properties (e.g. `SPACING` → a gap between children,
 `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` → size requests). Special `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` values: `-1` = FILL
 (expand to available), `-2` = HUG_CONTENT (native intrinsic size).
 
 > **Allocation semantics** — the exact meaning of a Fixed / `FILL` / `HUG_CONTENT`
 > size, how containers distribute space to children (main axis: only `FILL`
 > expands; cross axis: children hug unless `FILL`), and how content fits inside
 > a Fixed box, are defined in [LAYOUT.md](./LAYOUT.md).
 
 > **Units — logical points.** All size properties (`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`SPACING`/
 > `PADDING`/`CONTENT_MARGINS`, …) are expressed in an abstract **logical point**
 > unit — the same abstraction as SwiftUI points, Jetpack Compose `dp`, and CSS
 > pixels. A renderer MUST allocate the requested points box and fit content
 > within it; it must never treat the value as a device-pixel size. Each renderer
 > maps points to its native unit and resolves its own device resolution (logical
 > points × scale factor), so the same value yields the same physical size across
 > renderers.
 
 | Property | Value | Type | Native meaning |
 |----------|-------|------|----------------|
 | `SPACING` | `0x0001` | F32 | Gap between children |
 | `ALIGNMENT` | `0x0002` | F32 (enum code) | Cross-axis position (never stretches; default = Leading, `Fill`(3) = default hug — see LAYOUT.md) |
 | `CONTENT_MARGINS` | `0x0005` | F32 | Uniform inset between a stack's edge and its content |
 | `WIDTH` | `0x100B` | F32 | Width hint (-1 FILL, -2 HUG) |
 | `HEIGHT` | `0x100C` | F32 | Height hint (-1 FILL, -2 HUG) |
 | `GRID_COLUMNS` | `0x001E` | F32 | Grid column count (positive = count, -1/absent = auto-fit; a count, never a pixel width — see PRIMITIVES.md §Grid) |
 | `GRID_ROWS` | `0x001F` | F32 | Grid row count (positive = count, -1/absent = auto-fit) |
 | `GRID_TRACKS` | `0x0020` | STRING | Per-track grid spec (`flex`/`fixed:<pts>`/`adaptive:<pts>`, comma-separated) — takes precedence over the counts |
 
 #### Text properties
 
 Text-bearing nodes (`TEXT`, `BUTTON` labels, `TEXT_FIELD`) carry their content
 via `SET_TEXT` (0x03) and their layout via these properties:
 
 | Property | Value | Type | Native meaning |
 |----------|-------|------|----------------|
 | `TEXT` | `0x000A` | STRING | The text content (a `SET_TEXT`-style arena string) |
 | `LINE_LIMIT` | `0x000B` | U32 | Maximum number of lines (0 = unlimited) |
 | `TEXT_ALIGNMENT` | `0x000C` | F32 (enum code) | Alignment of the text block within its bounds |
 | `TRUNCATION_MODE` | `0x000D` | F32 (enum code) | Truncation style when text overflows (`Head`/`Middle`/`Tail`) |
 
 Enumerated values for these and every other enum-valued property are
 consolidated in [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md#appendix-enumerated-values).
 
 #### Styling properties (modifiers)
 
 Styling properties are **modifiers** — they apply to any view, not just stacks —
 and map to visual decoration rather than layout. `PADDING` (uniform) and its
 per-edge variants map to native padding, alongside
 `COLOR`/`BACKGROUND_COLOR`/`BORDER_*`:
 
 | Property | Value | Type | Native meaning |
 |----------|-------|------|----------------|
 | `PADDING` | `0x1011` | F32 | Uniform inner padding (any view) |
 | `PADDING_TOP` | `0x1012` | F32 | Top padding |

 | `PADDING_BOTTOM` | `0x1014` | F32 | Bottom padding |

 describes visual styling (hover/press styles stay renderer/token-owned).
 
 `STRING` properties carry their text in the frame's string section: the
 property value is the *relative* offset of a length-prefixed entry, exactly as
 `SET_TEXT`'s `B` field does.
 
 `TOGGLE` (`0x24`) is a boolean control whose visual style is a **token**, not a
 separate component: `TOGGLE_STYLE` (`0x2018`, ENUM) selects the native variant —
 `Switch` (sliding pill), `Checkbox` (square with checkmark), or `Button`
 (toggle button). The checked state is `SELECTED` (`0x2004`, U8 0/1), emitted
 guest → host and reported back host → guest. The renderer owns the visual
 presentation (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)).
 
 `SLIDER` (`0x25`) is a continuous numeric control: the guest emits its
 `VALUE` plus the `MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE` range, and the renderer reports value
 changes back as `VALUE_CHANGED` events (host → guest), resolving the semantic
 value from its own track geometry (see [EVENT](#event-0x03--host--guest)).
 
 ### EVENT (0x03) — host → guest
 
 The event commands and their `EVENT_LISTENERS` bits are catalogued in
 [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) (core events, SwiftUI-style); this file defines the
 wire encoding.
 
 Events are the **raw inputs**: the renderer reports what happened (a pointer
 went down/moved/up, a key went down/up) and resolves which node it hit via its
 own rendered-output tree. High-level interpretations — tap, drag, long-press —
 are built by the guest/app from these raw inputs and are **not** part of the
 protocol.
 
 #### Event listeners (which nodes emit events)
 
 A renderer reports raw events only for nodes that declared they want them. The
 application declares this intent through the `EVENT_LISTENERS` semantic
 property (`0x2005`, a u32 bitmask, `SET_PROPERTY` with the `U32` value type).
 Each bit requests a raw-input event kind (see [`listener`] flags):
 
 | Bit | Mask | Event command | Meaning |
 |-----|------|---------------|---------|
 | 0 | `0x00000001` | `POINTER_DOWN` | Report pointer-down for this node |
 | 1 | `0x00000002` | `POINTER_MOVE` | Report pointer-move/enter/leave |
 | 2 | `0x00000004` | `POINTER_UP` | Report pointer-up for this node |
 | 3 | `0x00000008` | `KEY_DOWN` | Report key-down |
 | 4 | `0x00000010` | `KEY_UP` | Report key-up |
 
 > Bits 5–10 (draft) are allocated in [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md#event-listeners-event_listeners)
 > for `FOCUS_CHANGED`, `EDITING_CHANGED`, `SUBMIT`, `SCROLL`, `WHEEL`, and
 > `VISIBLE_RANGE`. Value-bearing controls (`SLIDER`, `TOGGLE`, `DATE_PICKER`, …)
 > report their value changes by component type and do not need a listener bit.
 
 This is what makes **any element** (a `Text`, a `VStack`, …) able to emit
 events — the renderer attaches native input recognition to the matching native
 element when the listener bit is set, not only to buttons. A renderer SHOULD
 report `POINTER_DOWN`/`POINTER_UP` for a node with the `POINTER_DOWN`/
 `POINTER_UP` bits set by attaching a native click/press gesture to that
 element.
 
 | Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | Description |
 |---------|-------|---|---|---|-------|-------------|
 | `POINTER_DOWN` | `0x01` | targetId | x (f32) | y (f32) | `POINTER_SECONDARY` | Pointer button pressed at viewport-relative point |
 | `POINTER_MOVE` | `0x02` | targetId | x (f32) | y (f32) | `HOVER_ENTER` / `HOVER_LEAVE` | Pointer moved (bit 0 = entered/hovering, bit 1 = leaving) |
 | `POINTER_UP` | `0x03` | targetId | x (f32) | y (f32) | `POINTER_SECONDARY` | Pointer button released at viewport-relative point |
 | `KEY_DOWN` | `0x04` | targetId | keyCode (u16, low) | modifiers (u8, low) | `KEY_REPEAT` | Key pressed (bit 1 = auto-repeat) |
 | `KEY_UP` | `0x05` | targetId | keyCode (u16, low) | modifiers (u8, low) | — | Key released |
 | `VALUE_CHANGED` | `0x06` | targetId | value (f32) | 0 | — | A value-bearing control changed (e.g. slider); the renderer resolves the semantic value from its track geometry |
 | `TEXT_CHANGED` | `0x07` | targetId | string offset | 0 | — | A text field's value changed; the new text is a length-prefixed entry in the **event arena** (shared memory, absolute `B` offset) or the batch's string section (network, *relative* `B` offset) — the same dual convention as `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT` |

 #### Environment fields
 
 `META::ENVIRONMENT` is an **extensible field family** (mirroring
 `PARAMETER::SET_PROPERTY`): each opcode sets one platform environment field, so
 any number of fields ride one batch and new fields are new ids — never new
 commands. The platform (renderer / DOM client / SSR host) delivers the
 application's launch context this way; an HTTP request supplies what it offers,
 and the WebSocket connection **enriches** the environment after connect
 (viewport, native deep-links, and future fields all arrive the same way).
 
 | Field | Value | `B` encoding | Notes |
 |-------|-------|--------------|-------|
 | `VIEWPORT_WIDTH` | `0x0001` | f32 | Logical points |
 | `VIEWPORT_HEIGHT` | `0x0002` | f32 | Logical points |
 | `ROUTE` | `0x0003` | string offset | The initial route/deep-link path. String convention is the `TEXT_CHANGED`/`NAVIGATE` dual: absolute offset into the host → guest **event arena** over the shared ring, *relative* offset into the batch's string section over the network. |
 
 **Delivery** (spec DSL.md §4.5): on SSR the host synthesizes the environment
 from the HTTP request (`ROUTE` = request path — all the request offers); over
 the WebSocket the DOM client sends it (viewport + `ROUTE`) as its first message;
 a reconnect re-sends it. The application applies the environment uniformly — the
 router hydrates from the `ROUTE` field before mount, so a deep-link renders
 correctly on the first frame.
 
 #### Window metadata
 
 `META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA` is an **extensible field family** for presentation
 metadata of the host **window/surface** that owns the stream (a browser tab, a
 native window, an embedded surface). One opcode sets one field; new fields are
 new ids, never new commands. The protocol defines the concept; **each renderer
 maps it onto its own chrome** — the browser mapping is only one of them:
 
 | Renderer | `TITLE` | `DESCRIPTION` | `LOCALE` |
 |----------|---------|---------------|----------|
 | HTML / SSR | `<title>` | `<meta name="description">` | `<html lang>` |
 | DOM client | `document.title` | meta description | `<html lang>` |
 | GTK4 | window/headerbar title | accessible description | — |
 | Qt | window title | — | — |
 
 | Field | Value | `B` encoding | Notes |
 |-------|-------|--------------|-------|
 | `TITLE` | `0x0001` | string offset | Title of the hosting window/surface |
 | `DESCRIPTION` | `0x0002` | string offset | Human-readable description of the current content |
 | `LOCALE` | `0x0003` | string offset | BCP 47 content locale |
 
 The string encoding follows the same convention as `SET_TEXT`/`ROUTE`: an
 absolute offset into the guest arena over the shared ring, or a *relative*
 offset into the batch's string section over the network. An **empty string
 clears** the field, and the renderer applies its own default. Metadata is
 renderer-global (not part of the retained tree), survives `META::RESET`, and is
 re-emitted in a full snapshot (`META::RESYNC`).
 
 Semantics:
 
 - The application owns the values; a bound signal change emits exactly the
   changed field (like a property diff).
 - A proxied origin's window metadata is **ignored** — an embedded app never
   retitles the host window (spec/PROXY.md).
 - Web-only artifacts (`canonical`, `robots`, sitemap) are host concerns and are
   **not** protocol fields. A web renderer may accept them (plus Open
   Graph/Twitter/JSON-LD) as an **out-of-band render option** for one render
   call; this is renderer input, never guest state.
